HEADER.Description:
This model represents a dairy factory, processing fresh milk to produce a variety of products sold on the market: cream and cheese. It is made-up of 5 subprocesses: pasteurization, evaporation, cheese production, CIP and waste water treatment. 
As part of its waste streams, the factory discharges whey. Possible processes for valorizing this stream have been included in the analysis. They are the following: production of biogas through biodigestion or production of Rivella.

PasteurizationUnit.Unit Description: The pasteurization unit is responsible for the thermal treatment of raw milk to ensure microbial safety and product stability. In this process, fresh milk is heated to a controlled temperature  to eliminate pathogenic microorganisms, followed by rapid cooling to prevent degradation. During this operation, the milk is mechanically separated into skimmed milk and cream, which are directed to downstream processes. The pasteurization step is critical for meeting food safety standards and optimizing the performance of subsequent processing stages such as evaporation and cheese production.
PasteurizationUnit.Connectors Description: The pasteurization unit receives fresh milk as its main feed stream. Inside the unit, the milk undergoes controlled thermal treatment for heating  and cooling, ensuring microbial safety and product quality. Following thermal processing, the milk is separated into two main output streams: skimmed milk, which continues to downstream processing (e.g., evaporation), and cream, which is redirected for valorization in the mesost production line.
PasteurizationUnit.Heat Streams Description: The heat streams associated with the pasteurization stage include both hot and cold currents involved in heating and cooling the dairy product. The cold streams (HHX1, HHX2, and HT1) represent the progressive heating of the product—from refrigeration temperature up to the target pasteurization temperature—by recovering heat from outgoing hot fluids. The hot streams (CHX1, CHX2) correspond to product cooling after pasteurization, transferring heat back to the incoming cold streams through regenerative heat exchange. Additional hot streams such as CL1_ref and CL2_ref represent the use of a refrigerant to achieve the final cooling stage, ensuring the product returns to storage-safe temperatures. This heat recovery configuration improves thermal efficiency by minimizing external heating and cooling demands.
PasteurizationUnit.Equipments Description: The process involves several key pieces of equipment. Heat exchangers are used to transfer thermal energy between hot and cold streams, enabling the preheating of the feed and the recovery of heat from vapor streams. A separator is responsible for phase separation. A cooling tower dissipates excess heat to the environment, often used to cool recirculating water or process streams. Pumps ensure the transport of liquid streams throughout the system by maintaining the required pressure and flow rates.
PasteurizationUnit.Operating Cost Description: The fixed and variable operating costs includes manpower, fixed cost of operation, taxes etc.

EvaporationUnit.Unit Description: In dairy processing, evaporation is employed to concentrate milk or whey by removing a significant portion of its water content through partial vaporization.  Milk is preheated and introduced into the evaporator, where it flows over heated surfaces. Heat is supplied—usually via saturated steam in the shell side of the heat exchanger—causing water to vaporize. This unit operation increases total solids concentration, reduces volume for downstream processes such as spray drying, and improves product stability for storage or transport.
EvaporationUnit.Connectors Description: The connectors represent the mass streams involved in the milk evaporation process. The input stream is skimmed milk (SKIMMEDMILK), which feeds the system. The output streams include concentrated milk (CONCMILK), which is the desired product with a higher solids content; diluted whey (DILUWHEY); separated water (WATER), which exits at a higher temperature; and a wastewater stream (WASTEWATER) with low fat content. All streams are in the liquid phase and operate under the same temperature and pressure conditions (except for the heated water).
EvaporationUnit.Heat Streams Description: The heat streams represent the thermal energy exchanges within the evaporation process. They are categorized into cold streams, which receive heat and increase in temperature, and hot streams, which release heat as they cool down. The cold streams (e.g., HX1_c to HX7_c) correspond to process fluids being progressively heated, typically representing the preheating stages of the dairy feed. The hot streams (e.g., HX1_h, CL1_h_cw, and others) represent vapors or fluids releasing heat during condensation, cooling, or recovery. Each heat stream is characterized by inlet and outlet temperatures, enthalpy change, and heat capacity. A minimum temperature difference is applied for pinch analysis, and all streams assume a standard heat transfer coefficient.
EvaporationUnit.Equipments Description: The process involves several key pieces of equipment. Heat exchangers are used to transfer thermal energy between hot and cold streams, enabling the preheating of the feed and the recovery of heat from vapor streams. A separator is responsible for phase separation. A cooling tower dissipates excess heat to the environment, often used to cool recirculating water or process streams. Pumps ensure the transport of liquid streams throughout the system by maintaining the required pressure and flow rates.
EvaporationUnit.Operating Cost Description: The fixed and variable operating costs includes manpower, fixed cost of operation, taxes etc.

CheeseUnit.Unit Description:
This unit describes the cheese making process of the dairy factory. The process takes concentrated milk, salt and water as inlet,  and  produces cheese, and concentrated whey as co-product and brine as waste. Enzymes are added to the concentrated milk, allowing the separation of the curds and whey duirng the heating and separation steps. The curds are then shaped into the final cheese product and cooled, mixed with water and salt for flavor and preservation.  After the brining process, the cheese is separated from the brine. 
No aging step is considered in this specific process.
CheeseUnit.Connectors Description: The connectors represent the material streams involved in the cheese production process. The input streams include concentrated milk (CONCMILK), salt (SALT), and water (WATER), which are combined and processed to form the final product. The output streams consist of the finished cheese (CHEESE), which is a solid product with high fat and salt content, and by-products such as concentrated whey (CONCWHEY), rich in fat and water, and brine (BRINE), which contains dissolved salt.
CheeseUnit.Heat Streams Description: The heat streams in the cheese production process support both heating and cooling operations. The cold streams (HX1_c, HX2_c, and MIX1_c) correspond to the heating of dairy inputs through successive stages, raising their temperature in preparation for mixing or processing. The hot streams (CL1_h, CL2_h, and MIX1_h_c6 / MIX1_h_c7) represent the cooling of process fluids or mixed solutions, where thermal energy is released and partially recovered. These streams operate under controlled temperature differences, with standard heat transfer coefficients applied. Together, they reflect a thermally integrated process, balancing the energy required for heating with energy available from cooling
CheeseUnit.Equipments Description: The process involves several key pieces of equipment. Heat exchangers are used to transfer thermal energy between hot and cold streams, enabling the preheating of the feed and the recovery of heat from vapor streams. A separator is responsible for phase separation. A cooling tower dissipates excess heat to the environment, often used to cool recirculating water or process streams. Pumps ensure the transport of liquid streams throughout the system by maintaining the required pressure and flow rates.
CheeseUnit.Operating Cost Description: The fixed and variable operating costs includes manpower, fixed cost of operation, taxes etc.

CIPDairy.Unit Description: The CIP (Cleaning-In-Place) process is used to clean dairy equipment without disassembling it. Water and detergent solutions are circulated inside pipes, tanks, and machines to remove milk residues, fats, and proteins. First, the system is rinsed with water to remove loose residues. Then, a detergent solution is circulated for deeper cleaning. After that, the equipment is rinsed again to remove the detergent, followed by the application of a sanitizer to kill microorganisms. Finally, a last rinse with clean water removes any remaining sanitizer, leaving the equipment ready for use. This process ensures proper hygiene and safety in dairy production.
CIPDairy.Connectors Description: The system has a water inlet and a wastewater outlet, both with equal mass flow rates. Water enters at 25 °C and wastewater leaves at 30°C, both as liquid streams.
CIPDairy.Heat Streams Description: At the beginning of the process, the recycled and makeup water streams are mixed and heated to 80 °C. The water exits the process at 75 °C. Approximately 70% is recycled, while the remaining portion is cooled to 30 °C before being discharged.

MesostUnit.Unit Description: This unit describes the mesost making process of a dairy factory. The process takes cream, concentrated whey, and diluted whey as inlet,  and  produces mesost. Water is extracted from the process.
MesostUnit.Connectors Description: The MESOST process involves multiple input and output streams. The inputs include concentrated whey, diluted whey, and cream, each with distinct mass flow rates and compositions. The outputs consist of water from the CIP process and the final MESOST product. All streams are in liquid phase except for the CIP water, which is vapor. Detailed stream data are provided in the accompanying table.
MesostUnit.Heat Streams Description: The MESOST process includes several heat exchanger streams, classified as hot and cold. These streams represent the thermal energy transfers occurring within the system, facilitating heating and cooling steps necessary for process operation. Cold streams  absorb heat, while hot streams release heat. Some streams represent vapor-liquid phases or mixing points. Detailed thermodynamic and flow parameters for each heat stream are provided in the associated table.

BiodigesterUnit.Unit Description: The biodigestate unit in the dairy process handles the output from anaerobic digestion, where organic waste from the plant—such as wastewater, whey residues, or sludge—is biologically broken down in the absence of oxygen. This process produces biogas (mainly methane and carbon dioxide) and a liquid-solid by-product known as biodigestate. The biodigestate is separated and can be used as a nutrient-rich fertilizer or treated further depending on regulatory or environmental requirements. In this system, the biodigestate unit manages the flow, conditioning, and possible reuse or disposal of this material.
BiodigesterUnit.Connectors Description: The biodigestate unit receives two input streams: concentrated whey and diluted whey, both in liquid form. The outputs include two separate water streams, biogas, and solid fertilizer. Biogas is generated as a gaseous mixture of methane and carbon dioxide, while the remaining digestate is separated into water and a nutrient-rich solid fraction.
BiodigesterUnit.Heat Streams Description: The system includes several hot and cold process streams relevant for heat integration. Cold streams consist of boiler feedwater at different stages (HT1_boiler, HT2_boiler, HT3_boiler_fertilizer), which require heating for steam generation or further processing. Hot streams include wastewater (HT1_wastewater, HT2_cooler_wastewater) and biogas (HT1_biogas), which exit the process at elevated temperatures and offer heat recovery potential. Additionally, fertilizer process streams (HT3_V+L_fertilizer, HT3_L_fertilizer) involve vapor-liquid and liquid phases that release sensible and possibly latent heat, suitable for integration into the heat recovery network.
BiodigesterUnit.Equipments Description: The process involves several key pieces of equipment. Heat exchangers are used to transfer thermal energy between hot and cold streams, enabling the preheating of the feed and the recovery of heat from vapor streams. RivellaUnit.Unit Description: The Rivella unit processes whey-based streams to produce a functional beverage. In this unit, clarified and diluted whey is blended and conditioned, with precise control of temperature and composition. Additional steps may include pasteurization, carbonation, and the addition of natural flavors or other ingredients, depending on the product formulation. The final beverage is cooled and sent for packaging. This unit plays a key role in valorizing whey, a by-product of cheese production, by transforming it into a marketable drink.
RivellaUnit.Connectors Description: The Rivella unit receives multiple input streams, including diluted whey, concentrated whey, water, sugar, CO₂, and aroma, which are combined to produce the final beverage. These inputs contribute to the formulation, carbonation, and flavor profile of the product. The output streams consist of the finished Rivella beverage and a water stream used for CIP (Cleaning-In-Place) procedures. All connector data, including mass flow rates and compositions, are detailed in the accompanying table.
RivellaUnit.Heat Streams Description: The Rivella process includes a complex heat exchange network involving both heating and cooling steps for liquid and multiphase streams. Cold streams include preheating water to generate steam (HHX1_boiler_liquid and HHX1_boiler_vapor), as well as temperature conditioning for product and ingredient streams (e.g., MIX1 to MIX6). Hot streams represent heat sources such as condensate cooling (CL1, CL2, CL3), mixed-phase vapor flows, and process integration points with recirculating hot fluids (e.g., R6_hot_leaving).
